<jats:p>Using first-principles method, the work of adhesion (W<jats:sub>ad</jats:sub>) and electronic structure of Al<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>Hf (001)/Al (001) interface are studied and the mechanism of Al<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>Hf as enhanced heterogeneous nucleus of <jats:italic>α</jats:italic>-Al are discussed. The results indicate that
 Al + Hf-termination interfaces with same stacking sequence and the HCP (Al atom locating on top of the Al<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>Hf slab) interface with the same termination have maximum W<jats:sub>ad</jats:sub> and minimum interface energy (y<jats:sub>int</jats:sub>), and therefore they are more stable ones. It is noteworthy
 that Al + Hf-terminated interface with HCP is most steady one. The stacking of Al atoms on Al<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>Hf substrates tend to occur in this way. Besides, electronic structures indicate that Al + Hf-terminated interfaces have stronger electronic interaction than that of Al-terminated ones
 and the Al-Hf bonds of Al + Hf-terminated interface with HCP stacking tend to covalent bonds, while Al–Al bonds of Al-terminated one are metal bonds. Al<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>Hf as enhanced heterogeneous nucleation of <jats:italic>α</jats:italic>-Al are effective from crystallography and thermodynamics.</jats:p>
title: First-Principles Study on Al/Al<sub>3</sub>Hf Heterogeneous Nucleation Interface

title: Polymorphic Phase Transitions in Nanocrystalline Binary Metal Oxides
container-title: Journal of the American Ceramic Society

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Binary metal oxides occur in different polymorphic states under applied pressure and temperature. Structural changes occur due to polymorphic transitions in binary metal oxides. It is essential to theoretically predict the conditions of polymorphic transitions so that materials can be effectively used in engineering applications. Temperature and pressure are the two main factors affecting the bulk state phase transformation of materials. For nanomaterials, it has been observed that particle size and temperature are the main factors affecting the phase transformation, e.g., γ‐
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                      <jats:roman>Fe</jats:roman>
                    </jats:styled-content>
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                      <jats:roman>O</jats:roman>
                    </jats:styled-content>
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    to α‐
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                      <jats:roman>Fe</jats:roman>
                    </jats:styled-content>
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                      <jats:roman>O</jats:roman>
                    </jats:styled-content>
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    , monoclinic to orthorhombic transformation in
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">
                      <jats:roman>MoO</jats:roman>
                    </jats:styled-content>
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    , anatase to rutile transformation in Titania, γ to α Alumina transformation. We compile from literature the main factors which affect the phase stability of a nanocrystalline binary metal oxide. A heuristic approach to formulate particle size is put forth. Factors like surface energy, surface tension, and particle shape are considered, and a value for critical particle size is formulated. The model fits well with the experimental results for nanocrystalline alumina, titania, zirconia, and Fe
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    . Such an approach can be applied to predict the particle size‐dependent stability of a phase at known temperature range.
                  </jats:p>
title: Polymorphic Phase Transitions in Nanocrystalline Binary Metal Oxides
